issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly describes the dataset as a national probability sample and nationally representative/general population sample, but the Methods state participants were recruited from an introductory psychology participant pool at one university, with mean age 19 and overwhelmingly Pākehā. This is a student convenience sample, not a national probability sample. This mischaracterization fundamentally undermines claims of generalizability and the framing of the study as an advance over prior student-sample work.
issues.quote: We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington. ... Of the 374 participants included in this study, the average age was 19 years at Time 1 (2009; M = 19.42, SD = 2.31) and 68% were female. Furthermore, 76% of participants were born in New Zealand and the majority (86%) identified as Pākehā (New Zealand European).

issues.description: The title, abstract, introduction, and discussion present the study as a five-year analysis in a national probability/general population sample, but the actual sample is a small university participant pool. This is not a minor wording issue; it changes the implied external validity, novelty, and comparative interpretation versus prior student-sample work.
issues.quote: We examine the longitudinal influence of SDO and RWA on people’s willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment in a national probability sample over five years.

issues.description: The discussion and conclusion claim the findings are highly generalisable and nationally representative, which is incompatible with the described student sample. Such overclaiming may mislead readers about population-level inference.
issues.quote: Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.

issues.description: The manuscript inconsistently describes the environmental outcome as willingness to change behaviour, willingness to sacrifice, concern about environmental problems, pro-environmental attitudes, and environmentalism. These are distinct constructs. It is unclear what was actually modeled, which compromises construct validity and interpretation.
issues.quote: We examine the longitudinal influence of SDO and RWA on people’s willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment ...

issues.description: The Methods state environmentalism was measured as concern about environmental problems using two concern/exaggeration items, but the Data Analysis and Results repeatedly say the modeled variable was willingness to sacrifice for the environment. Table 1 labels the variable as WILL = willingness to make sacrifices for the environment. This is a direct inconsistency about the dependent measure.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley’s [28] environmental concern scale, “How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?” and “To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?” ... We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment.

issues.description: Environmentalism appears to be measured with only two items, and those items do not match the repeatedly discussed 'willingness to sacrifice' construct. Two-item scales are fragile, provide limited content validity, and require especially careful reporting of reliability and measurement invariance, which are absent here.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley’s [28] environmental concern scale, “How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?” and “To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?”.

issues.description: Longitudinal comparisons and cross-lagged paths assume that constructs are measured equivalently over time. The manuscript imposes equality constraints on some residual variances and structural paths, but does not report testing longitudinal measurement invariance for SDO, RWA, or environmentalism. Without invariance, apparent change/stability and cross-lagged effects may reflect changes in measurement properties rather than substantive relations.
issues.quote: We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant.

issues.description: One RWA item was not assessed at Time 2, yet the manuscript treats the construct as comparable across waves without describing how the missing indicator was handled in the measurement model. This undermines longitudinal comparability and may bias autoregressive/cross-lagged estimates.
issues.quote: The item “Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the “normal way” things are supposed to be done”, was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.

issues.description: The analyses used listwise deletion in a five-wave longitudinal study. This can substantially reduce effective sample size and bias estimates unless data are MCAR. Modern SEM software like Mplus supports FIML, which is generally preferred under MAR assumptions. No justification or missing-data diagnostics are provided.
issues.quote: Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion.

issues.description: A five-year panel requires clear retention/attrition information by wave, but the manuscript does not report how many participants remained at each time point, attrition rates, or whether attrition was selective. Directing readers elsewhere is insufficient for evaluating bias.
issues.quote: Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.

issues.description: Because only individuals who participated across five semesters were included, the analytic sample may be a highly selective subset of initial recruits. No comparisons of retained vs. lost participants are reported, threatening internal and external validity.
issues.quote: This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013). Of the 374 participants included in this study...

issues.description: The manuscript variously refers to five years, five semesters, and five time points spanning 2009 to 2013. Five semesters is not the same as five annual waves, and the lag interval matters for stationarity assumptions and interpretation of autoregressive/cross-lagged parameters. The timing is insufficiently and inconsistently described.
issues.quote: This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013).

issues.subcategory: use of traditional CLPM for causal claims
issues.description: The study uses a standard cross-lagged panel model and interprets coefficients causally. Traditional CLPMs conflate stable between-person differences with within-person change and can produce misleading cross-lagged effects. Random-intercept CLPM or related models would be more appropriate for separating within-person dynamics, especially when constructs are highly stable.
issues.quote: We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model ... These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism.

issues.description: The discussion repeatedly states or implies causal effects ('desire to dominate leads to lower environmentalism', 'causal pathway'), but observational longitudinal panel data do not establish causality, especially given possible omitted variables, measurement error, and the use of a CLPM. This overstates what the analyses can support.
issues.quote: These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism. The motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance, and to a lesser extent from the desire to submit to authority.

issues.description: The description of the path model is unclear and partly erroneous. It says residual variance was constrained 'for the same item over time', implying item-level modeling, yet the analysis is described as path analysis with three variables, and Table 1 reports scale-level reliabilities only. It is unclear whether latent variables, parcels, or manifest composites were analyzed.
issues.quote: We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time, so item 1 in the SDO scale had equal residual variance across all time points.

issues.description: The model constraint description repeats the same step twice ('constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point'), suggesting confusion in specification/reporting. This impedes reproducibility.
issues.quote: We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point. ... Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point.

issues.description: Reproducibility is limited because the syntax is only promised upon acceptance rather than provided during review or in supplementary material. Reviewers cannot verify model specification.
issues.quote: A copy of the Mplus syntax used will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript.

issues.subcategory: model fit acceptance despite poor fit
issues.description: The model has poor CFI (.86), yet the authors accept it because RMSEA and SRMR appear acceptable. Given the complexity and likely misspecification, accepting a poorly fitting model without sensitivity analyses or alternative models is problematic. Fit interpretation should be more cautious, especially with large degrees of freedom and possible measurement issues.
issues.quote: Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07), therefore the model was accepted.

issues.description: The model constrains parameters to be time-invariant because the authors were interested in 'overall' effects, but no comparison to less constrained models is reported. If cross-lagged effects differ across intervals, the stationary model can mask important variation or impose false equality.
issues.quote: We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects of SDO and RWA on changes in environmentalism, and not on whether these effects change during the interval measured.

issues.subcategory: low reliability of short ideological scales
issues.description: The reliabilities for SDO and RWA are low/modest, and the environmental measure reliability/invariance are not clearly reported. Measurement error attenuates and distorts structural relations. Using short forms may be unavoidable, but the consequences for longitudinal estimation should be addressed more thoroughly.
issues.quote: Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used, but are consistent with expectations based on previous research using short measures [31].

issues.description: Table 1 appears to report diagonal values for reliability, but the text only discusses SDO and RWA. Given the confusion around the environmental construct, reliability and exact scoring for the environmental measure should be explicitly reported and justified.

issues.subcategory: incorrect inference of stronger predictor despite non-significant difference
issues.description: The authors tested whether SDO and RWA differed in predictive strength and found the constrained-equality model did not fit significantly worse (p = .126), yet still conclude SDO is stronger based on coefficient magnitude. If the difference test is non-significant, claiming a stronger effect is not supported statistically.
issues.quote: We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA in our sample.

issues.description: Several chi-square difference statistics are missing the chi-square symbol or are garbled as '2(1)', making it unclear what was tested. One reported value (15,389.13) is implausibly huge relative to the tiny coefficients and likely reflects a reporting or computation error. These problems reduce confidence in the statistical reporting.
issues.quote: we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor ... 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126 ... the lagged effect on SDO was stronger than the reverse (2(1) = 39.97, p < .001) ... These lagged effects were also statistically different (2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001)

issues.description: Regression results report 'SD' for what are almost certainly standard errors. Confusing standard deviation with standard error is a reporting error that can mislead interpretation.
issues.quote: SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [-.13, -.09]) than RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001, 95% CI [-.05, -.01]).

issues.description: The manuscript relies on Figure 1 for key coefficients, but only a textual summary is provided here and no full parameter table is included. Replication and evaluation would require all autoregressive, cross-lagged, residual correlations, and fit-comparison results to be tabulated.
issues.quote: Figure 1. Unstandardized parameters assessing the association between SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice for the environment (WILL).

issues.subcategory: inferential leap from attitudes to motives
issues.description: The discussion infers motivational mechanisms ('desire to dominate', 'desire to submit to authority') from scale associations without directly measuring those motives in environmental contexts. This is stronger than the data support, especially given construct inconsistencies in the environmental measure.
issues.quote: The motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance, and to a lesser extent from the desire to submit to authority.

issues.description: The authors infer from one asymmetric cross-lagged finding that New Zealanders are socialized into authoritarianism more than social dominance. This is a broad sociopolitical conclusion not warranted by a small university sample and not directly tested.
issues.quote: Because we found that RWA predicts SDO over time, but SDO does not predict RWA, this suggests that New Zealander’s are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance.

issues.description: The Methods cite the NZAVS website for sample/procedure details, implying use of NZAVS data, yet the actual recruitment source is a Victoria University psychology pool. This creates confusion about the dataset provenance and whether NZAVS is the source at all.
issues.quote: We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington. ... Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.

issues.description: The introduction claims this study expands prior student-sample work by using a large national probability sample from the general population, but the sample described is itself a student sample. This undermines the manuscript’s central rationale and novelty claim.
issues.quote: We expand on Stanley et al.’s study by using a large, national probability sample spanning five years to examine how these variables relate over time in the general population.

issues.description: The manuscript refers to a 'large' sample, but the analytic sample is only 374 across five waves for a complex longitudinal SEM with many parameters. Given listwise deletion and item-level modeling implications, power and precision may be limited, especially for small cross-lagged effects.
issues.quote: We expand on Stanley et al.’s study by using a large, national probability sample spanning five years...

issues.subcategory: multiple testing / significance threshold rationale flawed
issues.description: The authors justify p < .05 by the large sample size, but large samples typically motivate emphasis on effect sizes and confidence intervals rather than relaxed thresholding. They also appear to switch to p < .01 in the figure note. No correction or coherent inferential strategy is described despite many paths/tests.
issues.quote: Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings.

issues.description: Methods state p < .05 as the significance threshold, while Figure 1 note states all parameters meet p < .01 unless otherwise noted. This inconsistency suggests an unclear analytic plan.
issues.quote: Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings. ... Figure 1. ... All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted.

issues.description: The two items described measure general concern and perceived exaggeration, not willingness to make behavioral sacrifices. If the modeled construct was indeed willingness to sacrifice, the item description is wrong; if not, the repeated interpretation in terms of sacrifice and behavior is invalid. Either way content validity is compromised.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems. ... “How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?” and “To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?”

issues.subcategory: no control for within-wave residual covariances clearly reported
issues.description: Cross-lagged models should typically include contemporaneous correlations/residual covariances among constructs at each wave. The manuscript does not clearly report whether these were estimated. Omitting them can bias cross-lagged paths.
issues.quote: We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment. The model included three variables across five measurement points...

issues.description: All measures use 7-point Likert scales, but the estimator and treatment of variables (continuous vs ordinal) are not reported. In SEM, estimator choice affects standard errors, fit indices, and parameter interpretation.
issues.quote: Participants rated the extent to which they agreed with each item on 7-point Likert scales...

issues.description: The manuscript does not state whether reverse-keyed items were recoded, how composites were formed, whether means or sums were used, or whether latent variables were modeled from items. These omissions hinder reproducibility.
issues.quote: Three items favoured dominance ... and three favoured equality, such as “We should have increased social equality”.

issues.description: Table 1 reports 95% confidence intervals 'based on 1000 iterations' for descriptive statistics/correlations, but the resampling method is not explained (bootstrap? Monte Carlo?). This is unusual and insufficiently documented.
issues.quote: Numbers in square brackets represent 95% confidence intervals based on 1000 iterations.

issues.description: The RWA cross-lagged coefficient is very small (B = -.02) and yet is discussed in broad theoretical terms about submission to authority and environmental exploitation. The substantive significance of such small effects is not discussed.
issues.quote: RWA was a weaker, but significant, negative predictor.

issues.description: The manuscript emphasizes statistical significance but gives little discussion of practical magnitude, especially for the small RWA effects and potentially small environmentalism-to-ideology effects. In longitudinal panel models with stable constructs, small coefficients may have limited substantive meaning.
issues.quote: The lagged effect of willingness to sacrifice on both SDO and RWA were statistically significant and negative...

issues.subcategory: confounding of environmentalism with climate change behavior
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly extrapolates from the measured environmental attitude variable to climate change denial, mitigation behavior, and communications strategy. These are related but distinct outcomes; the data do not directly test many of these claims.
issues.quote: Our findings highlight endorsers of SDO as targets for climate change communications.

issues.description: The manuscript cites a meta-analysis as [22] and a prior study as [24], but the wording around their findings and constructs is hard to reconcile with the current sample and measures. More importantly, there are inconsistencies in journal abbreviations and formatting that suggest insufficient editorial care, reducing confidence in reporting accuracy.
issues.quote: Stanley SK, Wilson MS. Meta-analysing the association between social dominance orientation, authoritarianism, and attitudes on the environment and climate change. J Env Psych. 2019.
